title: A Review of Psychological Literature on the Health and Wellbeing Benefits of Biophilic Design
review_question: To evaluate the evidence for each of the three Biophilic design experiences (Direct Experience of Nature, Indirect Experience of Nature, Experience of Space and Place) to support the theory that Biophilic design is beneficial for psychological wellbeing, focusing on environmental psychology literature and restorative environments.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Inclusion: Peer-reviewed academic journals, English language, Psychology field. Exclusion: Not related to environmental psychology and/or built environment.

findings.antecedent: Availability of natural light and windows
findings.quote: This quasi-experiment found that the availability of natural light and windows significantly improved mood and communication amongst nurses.

findings.antecedent: Daylight fluorescent lighting without windows in classrooms
findings.quote: children in rooms with daylight fluorescent lighting without windows had improved concentration when compared with children in classrooms with no windows

findings.antecedent: Views of water and sounds of water
findings.quote: water was found to be restorative.

findings.antecedent: Images of urban environment containing water
findings.quote: images of the urban environment that contained water were found to be even more preferred than nature images containing no water

findings.antecedent: Placing plants indoors
findings.quote: plants have a beneficial effect on stress reduction and pain tolerance.

findings.antecedent: Increased density of plants in an office setting
findings.quote: as the density of plants increased in an office setting, productivity decreased. At the same time, positive affect increased.

findings.antecedent: Green (including plants) office space vs. lean (minimalist) office space
findings.quote: perceived and actual productivity increased for occupants in a green (including plants) office space when compared with a lean (minimalist) office space.

findings.antecedent: Small, green, lightly scented plants
findings.quote: small, green, lightly scented plants were the most optimal for health and wellbeing.

findings.antecedent: Plants with red flowers
findings.quote: Plants with red flowers were found to be fatiguing after a period of time

findings.antecedent: Sunnier weather
findings.quote: People have been found to prefer sunnier weather and that this weather also is rated higher in terms of perceived restorativeness potential

findings.antecedent: Views to green trees (vs. brick wall) for gallbladder surgery patients
findings.quote: Patients who were recovering in a room with views to green trees recovered faster and required less pain medication than patients whose view was of a brick wall.

findings.antecedent: Green roofs (vs. non-vegetated/barren grey roofs)
findings.quote: green roofs have been found to be restorative.

findings.antecedent: Images of nature
findings.quote: Images of nature have been found to be as stress reducing as actual views of nature in certain circumstances

findings.antecedent: Mural views of nature with water (vs. actual 'mundane nature' views)
findings.quote: students perceived mural views of nature with water as the most restorative, even more than actual views of nature through a window of what Felsten calls "mundane nature"

findings.antecedent: Intermediate amount of wood (floor, one wall, furniture) in a patient room
findings.quote: The amount of wood in a patient room that was most preferred was an intermediate amount, with the floor, one wall and furniture being made of wood.

findings.antecedent: Fractals in natural environments
findings.quote: Fractals have been found in many natural elements... This could be an explanation as to why natural environments are often preferred over built ones

findings.antecedent: Nature with high levels of views and low levels of prospect
findings.quote: nature with high levels of views and low levels of prospect were deemed restorative

findings.antecedent: Places perceived to be highly restorative
findings.source: 4.3.2. Cultural and Ecological Attachment to Place
findings.quote: Places that are perceived to be highly restorative have been found to have strong place attachments for people

findings.antecedent: Natural environments
findings.source: 4.3.2. Cultural and Ecological Attachment to Place
findings.quote: natural environments, most likely due to their ability to afford restoration, have been found have a stronger attachment as a favourite place

findings.antecedent: Threatening encounters in nature
findings.quote: male individuals and those that are higher sensation seeker respond more positively to threatening encounters in nature than females

findings.antecedent: Images of abstract and nature art in office setting
findings.quote: images of abstract and nature art produced significant decrease in anger and stress in male office workers, but not female.

findings.antecedent: Indoor plants incorporated into a room
findings.quote: females demonstrated improved performance when plants were incorporated into the room when compared with males.

findings.antecedent: Biophilic-designed space (natural light, plants, natural ventilation, prospect and views, non-synthetic materials, recycled materials, open-plan workspace)
findings.quote: The preliminary results after three months indicate that the various benefits of Biophilic design are being realized in the space. This includes reduced stress, improved productivity, and improved wellbeing

synthesis_conclusions: There is significant evidence supporting certain attributes of Biophilic design, particularly the presence of natural elements like plants, water, and natural light, for human wellbeing.
Biophilic design, when considered through the lens of restorative environments, shows benefits for improved cognitive functioning, reduced stress, and improved mood.
The benefits of Biophilic design are being increasingly recognized and incorporated into green building rating systems like the Living Building Challenge and WELL Building Standard.
Individual differences in response to Biophilic elements, such as gender and sensation-seeking traits, need to be considered in design.
evidence_gaps: Empirical evidence for certain Biophilic attributes, such as the use of natural materials or processes, is lacking.
More research is needed on restorative environments beyond visual aspects, exploring other senses (auditory, olfactory) and natural light/materials.
There is a need for systematic reviews broadening the literature to psychology, health, planning, architecture, and engineering.
More research is needed to understand the specific contribution of different design features to wellbeing and sustainability.
Research on the various combinations of proposed Biophilic attributes and their combined impact is limited.
Further study is needed on how natural light and concentration in school children coincide with ART and SRT.

moderators.effect: Males and females respond differently to threatening nature, abstract/nature art for stress reduction, and indoor plants for creative task performance.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Males respond more positively to threatening nature and abstract/nature art for stress reduction. Females show improved creative task performance with indoor plants.

moderators.effect: Higher sensation seekers respond more positively to threatening encounters in nature.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Higher sensation seekers show more positive emotional responses to threatening nature.

moderators.variable: Type and amount of Biophilic feature
moderators.effect: The specific type and amount of natural elements (e.g., plant density, color of flowers, amount of wood) can modulate outcomes like productivity, affect, and preference.
moderators.subgroup_effects: High plant density can decrease productivity but increase positive affect. Red flowers can be fatiguing. Intermediate wood amounts are preferred.

limitations: The review is not exhaustive, and some attributes may have been studied in other fields outside psychology.
The majority of work on Biophilic design refers to environmental restoration theory as an underlying basis, limiting the scope to psychological literature examining this evidence.
The review primarily focused on the visual aspects of nature due to the prevalence of research in this area.

paper_metadata.title: A Review of Psychological Literature on the Health and Wellbeing Benefits of Biophilic Design
paper_metadata.crossref_title: A Review of Psychological Literature on the Health and Wellbeing Benefits of Biophilic Design
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Biophilic design has received increasing attention as a design philosophy in recent years. This review paper focused on the three Biophilic design categories as proposed by Stephen Kellert and Elizabeth Calabrese in “The Practice of Biophilic Design”. Psychological, peer reviewed literature supporting the benefits of Biophilic design was searched for through the lens of restorative environments. Results indicate that there exists much evidence supporting certain attributes of Biophilic design (such as the presence of natural elements), while empirical evidence for other attributes (such as the use of natural materials or processes) is lacking. The review concludes with a call for more research on restorative environments and Biophilic design.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Natural environments facilitate recovery from mental fatigue and restore directed attention, leading to improved cognitive function and wellbeing.
Exposure to natural environments reduces physiological and psychological stress, promoting relaxation and positive emotional states.
Humans possess an innate, genetically determined tendency to connect with nature and other living systems, which is essential for health and wellbeing.

mechanism_chain.description: Biophilic elements, such as natural light and views of nature, reduce stress and improve mood, which can enhance social interactions and communication.

steps.from_construct: Availability of natural light and windows / Views of nature
steps.to_construct: Reduced physiological arousal (e.g., lower heart rate, blood pressure)
